platforms.title: Burnout Isn't Just Being Tired
platforms.meta_description: Rest doesn't help and the exhaustion won't lift? How the WHO and mental health experts distinguish burnout from depression, and when to seek professional help.
platforms.body_html:
Rest doesn't seem to help, and the exhaustion just won't lift, so is this burnout or depression? The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies burnout not as a medical condition but as an 'occupational phenomenon'. Depression, on the other hand, is a medical condition that requires treatment. Without telling them apart, simply pushing through can mean missing a depression that actually needs care.

Why they look similar but are completely different

Burnout is an exhaustion tied directly to a specific job or situation. Common causes include an overwhelming workload, high-emotional-labor jobs like healthcare, teaching, counseling, or customer service, and repeated overtime. Even while feeling cynical and drained about work, someone with burnout can still find joy in hobbies or relationships unrelated to their job.

Depression is a mood disorder that shows up across life as a whole, regardless of work. A family history, a major stressful event, or a chronic illness raises the risk. Even hobbies that used to bring joy stop feeling interesting, and sadness or emptiness lingers most of the day for two weeks or more.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, whether the struggle is limited to work situations or spans life as a whole. Mental health experts note this is the clearest distinguishing sign. Burnout tends to ease up noticeably during a vacation, while depression rarely improves even with rest.

Second, whether taking time off actually leads to recovery. Burnout tends to noticeably improve within days to weeks once removed from the triggering workload. Depression tends to keep the exhaustion and sadness going even after plenty of rest.

What matters most is whether there's persistent worthlessness, hopelessness, or thoughts of self-harm or death. Those symptoms go beyond burnout, and call for professional help right away. Don't rely on a self-check list alone — if these signs are present, contact a mental health professional or crisis line without delay.

Recovery also looks different for each. Burnout tends to ease once the root cause itself changes, such as a reduced workload, more control over one's schedule, or a shift in role, alongside basic rest and firmer boundaries around work hours. Depression usually needs a different kind of care, typically therapy, sometimes medication, and consistent follow-up with a clinician, regardless of any change at work. Talking to a manager or HR about workload is a reasonable first step for burnout, while for depression the first step is usually a conversation with a doctor or therapist, since waiting it out alone can let the symptoms deepen.

Burnout and depression start as separate things, but leaving burnout unaddressed can lead into depression over time, meaning both can be present together. When it's hard to tell which one is going on, it helps to note whether the distress is limited to work situations, whether it improves with rest, and whether interest has faded in other areas of life too.

Does the exhaustion you're feeling ease up once you step away from work, or does it stay the same even after resting?
